prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current sequence learning methodologies, including many deep learning approaches, predominantly focus on memorizing concrete statistical dependencies between specific items. This reliance on concrete surface features leads to a significant limitation: the inability to form abstract representations. Consequently, these models suffer from memory inefficiency and struggle to transfer knowledge to novel sequences that share an underlying structure but differ in specific constituents. There is a lack of unified frameworks that can simultaneously compress data via chunking while also identifying and reusing abstract "variables" for generalization.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that rational sequence processing requires two complementary operations: **chunking** (characterizing temporal structure by grouping adjacent items) and **abstraction** (characterizing structural roles by identifying distinct items that function interchangeably). We posit that a generative model capable of explicitly representing "variables"—placeholders for categories of items with similar interaction properties—will achieve superior compression and allow for human-like transfer learning. By organizing these representations hierarchically, the system can trade off precise memorization for broader generalization.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a non-parametric Hierarchical Variable Model (HVM) that learns to parse sequences by iteratively discovering chunks and variables without supervision. The approach consists of the following conceptual modules:

1.  **Iterative Parsing and Dictionary Expansion:**
    The model will process sequences using a dynamic inventory of atomic units and learned patterns. Upon completing a parse, it will update transition statistics to propose new dictionary entries. This process will function recursively, allowing the discovery of increasingly complex, nested patterns layer by layer.

2.  **Dual-Mechanism Pattern Discovery:**
    *   **Chunk Proposal:** We will employ a mechanism to concatenate frequently occurring adjacent items into single distinct units ("chunks"), thereby compressing the sequence length.
    *   **Variable Discovery:** We will introduce a mechanism to identify "variables" based on contextual similarity. If distinct chunks are observed sharing the same preceding and succeeding contexts, the model will group them into a category (a variable). This variable acts as a higher-level symbolic placeholder that can be used in future chunk definitions.

3.  **Hierarchical Parsing Graph:**
    To ensure computational efficiency during retrieval, we will organize the learned dictionary into a hierarchical graph structure (akin to a prefix tree). This design will enable the model to rapidly identify the "deepest" or most specific pattern consistent with the incoming data stream by traversing common prefixes, rather than linearly scanning an expanding dictionary.

4.  **Abstraction-Based Composition:**
    New chunks will be formed not just by combining concrete items, but by combining existing chunks with variables. This allows the system to learn rules such as "Context A + [Variable X] + Context B," enabling the parsing of novel sequences where the specific instantiation of [Variable X] has never been seen in that exact sequence before.

## Expected Contribution
This research aims to bridge the gap between statistical pattern matching and symbolic abstraction. Theoretically, it will demonstrate how abstract concepts can emerge solely from the statistical properties of concrete sequences (specifically through context similarity). Practically, it will yield a memory-efficient sequence model capable of "zero-shot" transfer, where the agent can instantly process novel sequences by recognizing their familiar abstract structure, distinct from the behavior of standard large language models.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup
We designed a set of experiments to evaluate the Hierarchical Variable Learning Model (HVM) against baseline models in tasks involving sequence parsing, compression, and transfer learning.

*   **Generative Model Settings (Synthetic Data):**
    *   We utilized a probabilistic generative model to create sequences with nested hierarchical structures.
    *   **Inventory Expansion:** Iterations ($d$) = 30.
    *   **Atomic Units:** Size of atomic set $|A|$ = 10.
    *   **Sequence Length:** $|S|$ = 1000.
    *   **Probabilities:** Occurrence probabilities were sampled from a flat Dirichlet distribution ($\alpha_i = 1$).

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Synthetic Data:** Generated via the hierarchical generative model described above.
    *   **BabyLM Text Domains:** Random snippets of 1000 characters were drawn from four domains:
        *   CHILDES (Conversational child-directed speech).
        *   BNC (British National Corpus).
        *   Gutenberg (Narrative stories).
        *   Open Subtitles.
    *   **Human Behavioral Experiment Data:** 112 participants performed a sequence recall task.
        *   **Training Sequences (Control):** `BADF DCBF FEDB`.
        *   **Training Sequences (Variable Group):** `BXDF DXBF FXDB` (where `X` was `A`, `C`, or `E`).
        *   **Transfer Sequences:** `DXBF FXDB BXFD` (overlapping with training only at variable positions).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **HCM (Hierarchical Chunking Model):** Learns only chunks, no variables.
    *   **LZ78:** Standard dictionary-based compression algorithm.
    *   **Associative Learning (AL):** Updates first-order transitions between atomic units.
    *   **Large Language Models (LLMs):** Evaluated via in-context learning using prompt chaining:
        *   GPT-2
        *   Llama 2 (7B, 13B, 70B)
        *   Llama 3 (8B, 70B)

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Parsing Search Steps:** Number of comparison steps to locate the biggest chunk per parse.
    *   **Parsing Length ($|W|$):** Sequence length measured in chunks after parsing.
    *   **Sequence Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL):** $-\log P(S)$.
    *   **Coding Efficiency:** Ratio between dictionary size (number of entries) and original sequence length $|S|$.
    *   **Compression Ratio:** Number of tokens before compression divided by number of tokens after compression.
    *   **Recall Time:** Human time taken to recall the sequence.
    *   **Representation Complexity:** $\sum -\log P(u|v)$ (related to encoding cost).
    *   **Entropy:** Measure of uncertainty carried by embedded variables.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Significance Threshold:** Variable proposal occurred for correlations with $p \le 0.05$.
    *   **Memory Decay:** Parameter $\theta = 0.996$ used when modeling human behavior.
    *   **LLM Prompting:** Used instructions adapted from the human experiment (e.g., "Please remember the following sequence...").
    *   **Optimization:** Unused variables and chunks were deleted upon completion of each parsing iteration.

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Model Comparison on Alternative Sequences (BabyLM Domains)**
| Data Domain | Model | Compression Ratio | NLL (Negative Log-Likelihood) | Coding Efficiency |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| | HCM | 0.51 | 2783.71 | 0.05 |
| | HVM | 0.36 | 1953.01 | 0.06 |
| **BNC** | LZ78 | 0.39 | 3136.67 | 0.37 |
| | HCM | 0.65 | 3591.60 | 0.06 |
| | HVM | 0.50 | 3108.33 | 0.08 |
| **Gutenberg** | LZ78 | 0.39 | 3156.61 | 0.37 |
| | HCM | 0.69 | 3770.36 | 0.06 |
| | HVM | 0.54 | 3252.84 | 0.12 |
| **Open Subtitles** | LZ78 | 0.41 | 3395.09 | 0.39 |
| | HCM | 0.74 | 4151.89 | 0.07 |
| | HVM | 0.63 | 3764.48 | 0.07 |

**Correlation Data: HVM Likelihood vs. Human Recall Time**
| Phase | Metric | Value | p-value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Training Block | Pearson R | 0.86 | $\le 0.001$ |
| Transfer Block | Pearson R | 0.70 | $\le 0.001$ |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Synthetic Data Analysis**
*   **Parsing Search Steps:** We observed that organizing chunks in a parsing graph (HVM) dramatically reduced the average number of parsing search steps compared to HCM. The search steps for HVM scaled with the depth of the prefix tree, whereas HCM scaled with the size of the inventory.
*   **Sequence Length ($|W|$):** HVM transformed the sequence into a code size ($|W|$) much smaller than HCM and LZ78. HVM's parsing length was on par with the ground truth (GT) sequence length.
*   **Likelihood:** HVM parsed sequences with a higher likelihood (lower NLL) compared to HCM. This indicates variables recur more frequently than their specific representing chunks.
*   **Encoding Efficiency:** LZ78 created a larger dictionary than HVM and HCM to encode sequences of the same length. HVM and HCM (which harness hierarchical structure) encoded sequences more efficiently with smaller dictionaries.

**BabyLM Text Domain Analysis**
*   LZ78 consistently performed well on coding efficiency but created redundant dictionary entries.
*   HVM outperformed traditional compression (LZ78) in terms of compression ratio and negative log-likelihood in specific domains (e.g., CHILDES).
*   Across all four domains (CHILDES, BNC, Gutenberg, Open Subtitles), HVM compressed sequences further and parsed with lower complexity (NLL) than HCM.

**Human Behavioral Experiment**
*   **Human Performance:** The participant group trained on sequences with embedded variables recalled transfer sequences (which shared variables but differed in instance) faster than the control group.
*   **Model Correlation:** HVM sequence negative log-likelihood correlated significantly with human recall times during both the training and transfer blocks.
*   **Comparison to Other Models:**
    *   HCM and HVM exhibited lower sequence NLL after learning from a training block that shared variables.
    *   The Associative Learning (AL) model did not differentiate between training sequences that shared variables and those that did not.

**LLM Comparison**
*   **Training:** During the training block, the NLL of LLMs showed a stronger correlation with human recall times compared to AL or HCM.
*   **Transfer:** In the transfer block, cognitive models (HCM, HVM) demonstrated a much stronger correlation with human performance than the LLMs. HVM aligned most closely with human transfer behavior.
*   **Generalization:** All variants of the evaluated LLMs (GPT-2, Llama 2, Llama 3) failed to differentiate between training sequences that shared variables with the transfer block and those that did not, unlike humans and HVM.

**Abstraction, Distortion, and Generalization Trade-offs**
*   **Distortion:** As abstraction learning iterations increased, the representation graph became increasingly nested. This introduced more uncertainty (higher entropy) and distortion, consistent with Rate-Distortion theory.
*   **Generalization:** We observed that higher abstraction layers resulted in higher likelihoods (lower NLL) when parsing novel transfer sequences.
*   **HVM vs. HCM Transfer:** While HCM transfer performance improved with more chunk learning, it converged at a higher NLL than HVM. HVM's ability to learn variables allowed for more succinct compression of novel transfer sequences.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex
\begin{figure}[h]
\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}
\caption{Sample figure caption.}
\end{figure}
```

### Example Code for Tables
```latex

\caption{Sample table title}
\label{sample-table}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources
You may use only:
- The materials explicitly provided in this session.
- Logical reasoning derived from those materials.

#### Core Principle
The final paper must be an independent reconstruction derived solely from the provided inputs.  
This constraint is strict and overrides all other instructions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current sequence learning models, including standard chunking algorithms and large language models, primarily rely on identifying statistical co-occurrences to form representations. While effective for concrete pattern matching (chunking), these systems lack a mechanism for **abstraction**—specifically, the ability to identify contextually similar items and represent them as variables. Without this capability, models cannot distinguish between the structure of a sequence and its specific content. This leads to memory inefficiency (storing every variation as a unique pattern) and a failure to transfer knowledge to novel sequences that share a structural syntax but utilize different atomic constituents. We face a need for a unified cognitive framework that can simultaneously learn rigid chunks and flexible abstract variables from unsupervised data.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a **Hierarchical Variable Learning Model (HVM)**, a non-parametric Bayesian approach that serves as an approximate inverse to a hierarchical generative process. Our core hypothesis is that intelligent processing requires two distinct but complementary operations:
1.  **Chunking:** Concatenating frequently co-occurring items into stable units.
2.  **Variable Discovery:** Grouping distinct items that appear in identical contexts into abstract categories (variables).

By organizing these representations into a hierarchical **Parsing Graph (prefix Trie)** rather than a flat dictionary, we hypothesize that we can achieve logarithmic parsing complexity $O(D)$ rather than linear $O(|\mathbb{C}|)$, while explicitly separating structural syntax from concrete instantiation.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a probabilistic model that learns a belief set $\mathbb{B}$ comprising a dictionary of concrete chunks $\mathbb{C}$ and a set of abstract variables $\mathbb{V}$. The learning process will be iterative, alternating between parsing the observation sequence and updating the dictionary via hypothesis testing.

### 1. Representation Structure: The Parsing Graph
Unlike standard chunking models, we will organize memory items in a hierarchical **Parsing Graph (PG)**. This graph will be structured as a prefix Trie where each node represents a chunk, and a parent node represents the common prefix of its children.
*   **Nodes:** Chunks $c \in \mathbb{C}$.
*   **Edges:** Transitions between prefixes.
*   **Retrieval:** To parse an incoming sequence, the model will traverse the graph from the root to the deepest node consistent with the upcoming observations.

### 2. Sequence Parsing and Matrix Updates
The model will parse the sequence $S$ into a series of units $c_1, c_2, \dots, c_N$. During parsing, we will maintain and recursively update two key matrices:
*   **Transition Matrix ($T$):** Tracking the frequency of adjacent chunks.
*   **Marginal Frequency Matrix ($M$):** Tracking the occurrence of individual chunks.

For a parsed transition from chunk $c_L$ (left) to $c_R$ (right) at time $t$, the update rule is:
$$ T_{ij}(t+1) = \theta \cdot T_{ij}(t) + [i = c_L][j = c_R] $$
$$ M_{i}(t+1) = \theta \cdot M_{i}(t) + [i = c] $$
where $[ \cdot ]$ is the Iverson bracket (1 if true, 0 otherwise) and $\theta$ is a memory decay parameter.

### 3. Mechanism I: Chunk Proposal (Concatenation)
We will define the probability of a chunk $c_i$ based on the marginal counts:
$$ P_{\mathbb{C}}(c_i) = \frac{M_i}{\sum_{c_j \in \mathbb{C}} M_j} $$
We will start with the null hypothesis $\mathcal{H}_0$ that consecutive chunks $c_L$ and $c_R$ are statistically independent, i.e., $P(c_L, c_R) = P(c_L)P(c_R)$. We will perform a hypothesis test (significance level $p=0.05$). If the null hypothesis is rejected, we merge $c_L$ and $c_R$ into a new chunk:
$$ c_{new} = c_L \oplus c_R $$
This new chunk is added to $\mathbb{C}$ and inserted into the Parsing Graph as a child of the node representing $c_L$ (or the longest shared prefix).

### 4. Mechanism II: Variable Discovery (Abstraction)
The critical innovation is the identification of **variables**—abstract entities representing sets of chunks that appear in the same context.
*   **Context Definition:** A context is defined by the preceding chunk $c_{pre}$ and succeeding chunk $c_{post}$.
*   **Proposal Logic:** We will identify variables by computing the intersection of the post-adjacency columns and pre-adjacency rows in the transition matrix $T$.
*   **Formulation:** If a set of chunks $\{c_1, \dots, c_j\}$ significantly correlates with specific neighbors, we propose a variable $v$ such that the denoting set is $E(v) = \{c_1, \dots, c_j\}$.

We define the probability of the variable constituents as:
$$ \sum_{c \in E(v)} P(c | v) = 1 $$

If a variable $v$ is identified, we propose a new abstract chunk structure:
$$ c_{abstract} = c_{pre} \oplus v \oplus c_{post} $$
This allows the model to compress multiple sequences (e.g., $A\text{-}B\text{-}C$ and $A\text{-}D\text{-}C$) into a single abstract representation $A\text{-}v\text{-}C$ where $v \in \{B, D\}$.

### 5. Representation Complexity and Optimization
To manage the trade-off between compression and abstraction, we will define **Representation Complexity (RC)** to measure the nestedness of the learned variables:
$$ RC(\mathbb{V}) = \sum_{v \in \mathbb{V}} \sum_{u \in E(v)} - \log P(u | v) $$
We will implement a "Representation Cleaning" phase at the end of each iteration, where unused variables and chunks are pruned to ensure the dictionary remains compact.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Unified Cognitive Architecture:** We expect to provide the first computational model that integrates chunking (concrete memory) and variable binding (abstract memory) within a single non-parametric Bayesian framework.
2.  **Algorithmic Efficiency:** By introducing the Parsing Graph, we aim to reduce parsing time complexity from linear w.r.t dictionary size to logarithmic (scaling with tree depth), enabling scalability to larger datasets.
3.  **Generalization Theory:** We expect to demonstrate that learning variables allows for "zero-shot" transfer to novel sequences that satisfy the structural logic of the training data but utilize different tokens, a capability lacking in standard associative learning models.

notes.permissions: --permission-mode bypassPermissions (container and shield are the boundary)
notes.extra_model_calls: WebFetch runs a secondary extraction model call inside Claude Code; counted in modelUsage
notes.telemetry: telemetry, error reporting and nonessential traffic disabled; this also stops feature-flag fetching

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
